items.internal_ref: H08 (fresh-batch-1, engine Z) — R1 decomposition-coverage miss target
items.source_snapshot:
When the best decision is no decision: the rise of randomization in grant funding

Rachel Heyard’s job was to find a signal in the noise, but the trouble was how often there wasn’t one. As a biostatistician in the data team at the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) in Bern, Switzerland’s main public research funder, Heyard faced a tricky problem. Reviewers and panel members scored each grant application against criteria such as scientific relevance, feasibility and the applicant’s track record, grading the proposal on a scale from A to D. Her team’s task was to test how much those scores could be trusted: to determine which applications truly outranked the others in the competition for limited funds.

The strongest and the weakest proposals were sorted readily enough. But the rest piled up in the messy middle — what she calls “a cloud of B proposals” — clustered so tightly in score that panels struggled to differentiate them. To force a ranking, they sharpened the grades with pluses and minuses, splitting hairs that might not have existed.

Heyard helped to build a statistical framework to measure what the reviewers’ scores were actually worth. It treated each proposal’s standing not as a fixed rank, but as a range that reflected the uncertainty in a panel’s judgement. Instead of pretending that one proposal was exactly 23rd and another precisely 27th, the model asked whether those apparent ranks could really be distinguished.

Near the funding line, they often could not.
items.candidate_sentence: The specific limit built into this classification is that the scale's resolution was treated as adjustable by the raters, when in fact resolution is a property of the underlying signal — and the signal, near the funding line, was not there to be resolved.
items.rationale_internal_not_shown_to_reviewer: H08 target — B2-v2's R1 (proposition-decomposition) stage never produced a claim_id for this exact sentence in the real recovery run, so no downstream stage could ever audit it; a decomposition-coverage miss, not a support/role disagreement. Round 001 asks whether an independent human, given only the source + this sentence, reads it as adding an unestablished fact (the scale's resolution being a property of the underlying signal, not the raters' choice) — testing whether ordinary human reading converges with the miss B2 should have caught.

items.internal_ref: H17 (fresh-batch-1, engine Z) — R1-factual/R2-interpretive hedge conflict
items.source_snapshot: The National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) plans to fund an extra 12,000 projects through its Young Scientists Fund. Under NSFC rules, male applicants must be under 35 years old and female applicants under 40. This raises a wider question for science funders: should early-career support be tied to birthdate?
items.candidate_sentence: The differential cutoffs reveal that the system is not purely measuring career stage at all — it is measuring career stage adjusted for an assumed sex-linked career disruption pattern (e.g., childbearing).
items.rationale_internal_not_shown_to_reviewer: H17 target — B2-v2's R1 says empirical_dependency=true (a real dependency exists); R2 independently calls the claim interpretive_only, citing the claim's own hedge/parenthetical ('e.g., childbearing') as exemption grounds. This is the single most-repeated real failure across v1.3/v1.4.1/v2 (FLAGGED_NOT_RESOLVED, unchanged across the R2 capacity-recovery run). Round 001 asks whether a human reader is also swayed by the hedge, or reads the sentence as adding something the short source snippet never establishes.

items.internal_ref: H14 (fresh-batch-1, engine S) — support-strength calibration target
items.source_snapshot:
The US National Institutes of Health (NIH) has begun turning away research grant applications for which the “primary function” is informing policymakers and legislators, according to internal documents seen by Nature. This means that the agency is likely to fund fewer projects assessing how public policies affect human health.

“Policymakers are not considered a stakeholder group within the scope of NIH’s mission,” the internal documents say.

Dozens of applications have since been sent back to NIH programme officers in charge of the proposals, instructing them to remove the word ‘policy’ and its derivatives and determine whether the proposals can be salvaged, two NIH officials say. More than 3,700 projects funded during the 2025 fiscal year include these words in the project title or abstract, according to the NIH’s project database.
items.candidate_sentence: But the 3,700+ already-funded projects expose what this assumption costs: the word is not decorative in those titles and abstracts; it is load-bearing, marking the orientation of the work toward its intended use.
items.rationale_internal_not_shown_to_reviewer: H14 target — R1 and R2 AGREE on role (factual_dependency) and support (unsupported) for this exact claim in the recovery run; the open question is a different one — a separate run of the same architecture (Regression #1) put this same claim at 'supported' instead, a documented run-to-run support-strength variability, not a role/decomposition problem. Round 001 asks a human the same source-support question independent of that internal variability.

items.internal_ref: H05 (fresh-batch-1, engine M) — second R1-factual/R2-interpretive conflict, same source family as slot 1
items.source_snapshot:
When the best decision is no decision: the rise of randomization in grant funding

Rachel Heyard’s job was to find a signal in the noise, but the trouble was how often there wasn’t one. As a biostatistician in the data team at the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) in Bern, Switzerland’s main public research funder, Heyard faced a tricky problem. Reviewers and panel members scored each grant application against criteria such as scientific relevance, feasibility and the applicant’s track record, grading the proposal on a scale from A to D.

The strongest and the weakest proposals were sorted readily enough. But the rest piled up in the messy middle — what she calls “a cloud of B proposals” — clustered so tightly in score that panels struggled to differentiate them. To force a ranking, they sharpened the grades with pluses and minuses, splitting hairs that might not have existed.

Heyard helped to build a statistical framework to measure what the reviewers’ scores were actually worth. Instead of pretending that one proposal was exactly 23rd and another precisely 27th, the model asked whether those apparent ranks could really be distinguished. Near the funding line, they often could not.

Starting in 2022, the SNSF stopped treating these rankings as exact. A mathematical model identified the proposals that were too close to separate and sent them into a lottery. Peer review still set the bar to qualify, but among the proposals near the funding threshold, a financed project and a rejected one would be decided by chance.
items.candidate_sentence: The invisible work was not evaluation; it was the manufacture of the appearance of evaluation.
items.rationale_internal_not_shown_to_reviewer: H05 target — a second, independent instance of the identical R1-factual/R2-interpretive-hedge failure shape as item 2 (H17), from a different candidate/engine on a related but not identical passage of the same source article. Chosen over H03 to avoid presenting the reviewer the exact same 900-character source snapshot twice in one 5-item session (H17/H03 share an NSFC source excerpt short enough that a repeat would likely be noticed and could bias the reviewer toward hunting for a 'trick').

items.internal_ref: 05_dutch_painting_soldier/Z (development set, De Hooch) — CONTROL: R1/R2 agree, clean adjudication
items.source_snapshot:
Two’s company, three’s a crowd. Perhaps that was the logic someone used hundreds of years ago when altering Pieter de Hooch’s A Man Smoking and a Woman Drinking in a Courtyard (1658-60) by painting over the image of a beer-wielding soldier, removing him from the presence of the two other main figures.

The Netherlands-based Mauritshuis art museum recently revived the original vision laid out by de Hooch, a 17th-century painter who mastered portrayals of domestic life during the Dutch Golden Age. Conservators decided to paint the missing man back into the scene and rename the artwork Figures in a Courtyard.

“[It] is now much more moralistic,” Judith Niessen, the head of collections and research at the Mauritshuis, tells the Art Newspaper’s Senay Boztas, “which was the intention of de Hooch.”

“With only the man and the woman at the table, the painting seems to be way more innocent than with the second man present,” Niessen tells the Art Newspaper. “Where she would be just drinking a glass of beer before, now it is much more obvious that they are playing a drinking game, where she is drinking the pass-glass and the two men are not.”
items.candidate_sentence: De Hooch's moralism functioned through contrast and implication: the woman drinking the pass-glass while the two men abstain is the moral signal, not mere depiction of drinking.
items.rationale_internal_not_shown_to_reviewer: 05_dutch_painting_soldier/Z (De Hooch) CONTROL — R1 and R2 fully agree (r1_agreement='consistent') that this claim is factual_dependency/unsupported; a clean, non-contested internal adjudication. Chosen over an NSFC/SNSF-source control to give Round 001 topic diversity (art history, not grant funding) and because the target claim ('the contrast IS the moral signal') is a self-contained causal/mechanism claim that a non-specialist can evaluate without domain knowledge — a good test of whether human over-selection of 'adds unestablished' generalizes beyond the grant-funding domain, or whether humans converge with the system's own agreement here.
